DON'T PANIC

All Tied Up II: Lotsa Knots

Start here: the second drawer of the string toolbox

Volume I — Tying It All Together, Explained — taught the basics: a bowline, a figure-eight, two half hitches, a trucker's hitch, and how a ratchet strap thinks. This book assumes those are in your hands already. If they aren't, go back; everything here is built on them and nothing here re-teaches them.

These are the medium-advanced knots: loops in the middle of a rope, joins that stay joined, hitches that grip a line itself, and lashings that build structures. The hardest rigging — pulleys, mechanical advantage systems, and the advanced tricks — is deliberately NOT here. That is the next book's job.

THE ONE RULE, AGAIN: no knot in either book is a licence to hang a person. These knots move gear, shelter, food, and loads. Climbing and rescue are their own disciplines with their own rated gear and training. A knot you learned from a book — this one included — is not that.

How to check any knot in this book

Four checks, in order, every time — the same four the diagrams show. Dress it: arrange every strand neat, flat, and side by side; a sloppy knot is a weak knot wearing a disguise. Set it: pull each part in the direction it will be loaded, one at a time. Test it: load it gradually — lean on it, don't leap on it — and watch for creep. Back it up: where a tail can work loose, finish it with a stopper knot from Volume I.

And the untie question, asked before you tie, not after: how does this come undone? Every entry below answers it. A knot you cannot untie is a knife problem waiting to happen.

2. Alpine Butterfly

For: a strong loop in the MIDDLE of a rope, with no end needed — isolate a worn section, clip a load mid-line, make a handhold.

Never for: tying two ropes together, or a loop that must open flat against a surface.

Check / untie: The finished knot looks like a butterfly: two wings, loop on top. It unties after loading by bending the wings back. If the wings are uneven, re-dress it.

3. Double Bowline

For: a fixed end loop that stays put even in stiff or slippery rope — the bowline's stronger twin.

Never for: mid-line loops (use the Butterfly), or anywhere a shrinking loop is actually wanted.

Check / untie: Two wraps around the standing line before the rabbit comes back down. Back it up with a stopper in the tail in slippery rope. Untied like a bowline: push the collar back.

4. Bowline on a Bight

For: a double loop at the end of a rope, tied without the end — two legs to spread a load, or an emergency chair of loops for GEAR.

Never for: lifting people as a planned system — this book does not rig for people, full stop.

Check / untie: Both loops should come out the same size; adjust before loading by feeding rope through the knot. Collapses flat to untie once the load is off.

5. Figure-Eight Follow-Through

For: tying a rope AROUND an anchor — a tree, a closed ring — when the end must be threaded and the knot retraced.

Never for: joining ropes quickly in the cold; a sheet bend or double fisherman's is faster to check.

Check / untie: Trace with your finger from end to end: the second strand must parallel the first everywhere, with no twists. A crossed trace is a re-tie, not a fix.

6. Directional Figure-Eight

For: an in-line loop that takes load along ONE direction of the rope — a haul line's pulling loop.

Never for: loads that can swing to pull from the side or the other direction; it can roll and fail. Use the Butterfly for multi-direction pulls.

Check / untie: The loop must point the way the load will pull. Mark the loaded direction in your head before you trust it, and test with a steady lean of body weight on GEAR only.

7. Double Fisherman's

For: joining two ropes — especially thinner cord — into one long line that stays joined; the classic cord-loop knot.

Never for: thick, stiff rope (it jams and wastes length) or joins you must undo often; it tightens hard under load.

Check / untie: Two neat barrel knots pulled face to face, tails a thumb long. To untie after light loads, work each barrel loose with your thumbs; after heavy loads, accept it may be permanent.

8. Water Knot

For: joining WEBBING and straps — the flat-material join; also re-joining a strap whose buckle is gone.

Never for: round rope as your first choice (use a double fisherman's), or webbing with short tails — this knot creeps.

Check / untie: Tails must be at least a hand long, and the knot re-checked after the first load: water knots walk loose over time. Trace it flat, no twists in the webbing.

9. Zeppelin Bend

For: joining two ropes that MUST come apart again afterwards — the bend that stays put under load, then unties with a wiggle even after it has been hauled on. Two loops, one like a 6 and one like a 9, interlock; each end passes through both loops.

Never for: joining webbing (use a water knot), or with short tails — leave a hand's length on both ends, because the tails are what you pull to untie it.

Check / untie: the finished bend is symmetrical, like two loops shaking hands. Pull the standing parts to set it — never the tails. To untie, push the two loops apart and wiggle; it lets go even after a serious load, which is the whole reason it exists.

10. Anchor Hitch

For: tying a rope to a ring or anchor that will stay loaded for a long time — it snugs down and stays dressed.

Never for: a post you need to release under load; it can jam tight. A round turn releases easier.

Check / untie: The two turns around the anchor take the load; the hitches just lock them. If the turns are loose, the lock does all the work and will slip — re-wrap.

11. Constrictor Knot

For: a binding that bites and does not let go — hose clamps from string, whipping a rope end, closing a sack neck.

Never for: anything living, anything you must untie, anything soft it can cut into. It is close to permanent.

Check / untie: Often the honest way to remove it is to cut it off, sliding the blade under the crossing strand against a hard surface. Tie it knowing that.

12. Prusik Hitch

For: a cord loop that slides along a main line when loose and GRIPS it when loaded — adjustable anchor, progress keeper on a haul.

Never for: a main line caked in mud or ice (it slides when it should grip), or shock loads. Never as a brake for a person.

Check / untie: Use cord clearly thinner than the main line. Dress the wraps neat — crossed wraps halve the grip. Test the grip with a hard hand pull before trusting it with a load.

13. Klemheist Hitch

For: the Prusik's one-way cousin: grips when pulled one way, made from a webbing or cord loop — handy when your cord is a strap.

Never for: pulling in the wrong direction (it is directional — the wraps must face the load), or on icy line.

Check / untie: All wraps must lie the same way, like a coil spring. If it slips, add a wrap; if it jams solid, take one off. Test before loading, every time.

14. Rolling Hitch

For: gripping a line — or a pole, or a pipe — so you can haul ALONG it: pulling a load sideways off a jammed line, towing, or taking the strain while you re-tie something. Two wraps cross over its own standing part, which is what stops it sliding back.

Never for: a pull that comes away from the line at an angle — it is built to grip along the line, toward the wraps, and a sideways pull rolls it loose. For a grip that holds in any direction on a rope, use a prusik.

Check / untie: haul toward the wraps, and test the grip with a steady pull before you trust it — on smooth or icy line, add a third wrap. It unties like the half hitches it is made of: slack it off and unwrap.

15. Square Lashing

For: joining two poles where they cross at a right angle — the corner of every frame, shelf, gate, and shelter skeleton in the aftermath. The most common lashing there is: clove hitch to start, square wrapping turns around both poles, frapping turns between them to cinch it drum-tight.

Never for: poles that cross at an angle — that is a diagonal lashing's job, and square wraps on an angled crossing will walk and loosen. On smooth, slick poles, roughen or notch the contact point first.

Check / untie: grab both poles and try to twist the joint — it should feel like one piece of wood. Sloppy, crossed wraps are the usual failure: neat and side by side is strength, not tidiness. Unties by unwrapping in reverse; a lashing that was loaded hard may need the frapping turns cut.

16. Diagonal Lashing

For: joining two poles that CROSS at an angle — braces, gates, and frames that want to rack sideways.

Never for: poles that meet end-to-end (that's a different join) or with frayed rope; diagonal lashing eats rope fast.

Check / untie: The X-wraps pull the crossing tight first, then the horizontal wraps lock them. If the joint racks, your frapping was too loose — re-frap, don't just add wraps.

17. Tripod Lashing

For: three poles into a tripod — a pot stand, a shelter apex, a signal mast base.

Never for: uneven ground without levelling the feet first; a tripod is honest about slopes.

Check / untie: Lay the three poles side by side, lash at the tops, then spread the feet and let the wraps settle into the crossing. Set it, load it gently, then re-check the lashing before the pot goes on.

18. Tensionless Hitch

For: anchoring a line to a smooth post or tree so the FULL strength of the rope does the holding — wraps, not knot, carry the load.

Never for: skinny or rough anchors (the rope can slide off or saw into bark), or anywhere you can't make at least three full wraps.

Check / untie: It only works if the wraps stay put and the final hitch just keeps the tail from unwinding. Protect tree bark with padding — a dead tree helps nobody.

19. Round Turn and Two Half Hitches

For: securing a loaded line to a post so it can be ADJUSTED or released while still holding — the thinking person's tie-off.

Never for: leaving a critical load on it unattended for days; check and re-set it like every hitch.

Check / untie: The round turn is the brake: keep a hand on the tail and the load behaves. Release a little at a time, never all at once, and never with fingers between rope and post.

20. What to scavenge for the advanced drawer

Volume I's scavenging list still applies — rope, straps, bungees, and ties are the base layer. This book adds a second drawer:

  • Retired climbing and marine rope — For utility loads only, never for a person — unknown history is unknown history (Volume I, Entry 3). The best lashing and hauling rope you will find.
  • Tubular webbing — Climbing-shop offcuts and old slings. Flat, strong, and the water knot's home turf.
  • Paracord and strong cord — Prusik loops, guylines, lashing. Thinner than your main line is a feature, not a flaw — friction hitches need it.
  • Carabiners, rated — Stamped with a rating or they are keychains. For clipping loads to loops — quick, strong, and they save rope.
  • Spare ratchet and cam straps — Webbing donors for water knots and klemheists, even when the ratchet itself is dead.
  • Wooden poles and dowels — Broom handles, tool handles, straight branches. Lashing practice now, tripods and ladders later.
  • Zip ties and cloth tape — For marking tails, bundling cord, and taping rope ends so they cannot fray mid-knot.

Field recipes: the advanced drawer at work

Field Recipe · Rope Ladder

Makes: a way up to a loft, a roof edge, or out of a pit — for gear first, and for people only as a last-resort aid with a spotter, never as a plan.

You need: two long ropes of equal length, short poles or stout sticks for rungs, one strong anchor above.

  1. Anchor both ropes at the top with anchor hitches, a body's width apart. The ladder is only ever as good as this anchor.
  2. Tie the top rung in with two constrictor knots, one on each rope — rungs must not slide, and constrictors do not slide.
  3. Work down: a rung every knee-height, each tied with constrictors, checking the ladder hangs straight as you go.
  4. Weight the bottom rung with a heavy object so the ladder hangs still instead of dancing.
  5. Test each rung with a hard downward pull before anyone trusts it with weight.

Field Recipe · Hammock Hang You Can Trust

Makes: two trees, one hammock, no 3 a.m. meeting with the ground.

You need: one hammock, two lengths of webbing or rope, two rated carabiners if you have them.

  1. Wrap each tree with webbing and join it with a water knot, tails a hand long — flat webbing spreads the load and spares the bark.
  2. Clip or tie the hammock ends to the webbing loops at hip height; a hammock hung like a banana sags to sitting height.
  3. For rope instead of webbing: a tensionless hitch at each tree, finished and checked.
  4. Sit down slowly, in the middle, first time. Creep shows itself in the first minute, not the fifth hour.

Field Recipe · Tripod for a Camp Pot

Makes: a stand that holds a pot over a fire and folds flat when you move.

You need: three poles of equal length, one length of rope, one pot with a bail handle.

  1. Lay the three poles side by side and join their tops with a tripod lashing (Entry 17).
  2. Stand the tripod up, spread the feet wide on level ground, and let the lashing settle into its crossing.
  3. Hang the pot from the apex with a short cord and an alpine butterfly loop to adjust the height over the flame.
  4. Re-check the lashing after the first boil — heat, steam, and shifting feet all loosen wraps.

Field Recipe · Adjustable Guylines for a Tarp in Wind

Makes: a tarp that stays pitched when the weather argues.

You need: cord for each tarp corner, stakes, one tarp.

  1. Tie each corner cord to the tarp with a bowline on a bight if the corner is doubled, or Volume I's basics for single corners.
  2. Halfway down each cord, tie a prusik loop around the cord itself running to the stake — slide it to tension, and it grips under load.
  3. Stake lines at 45 degrees, prusiks slid up until every line sings the same note.
  4. After the first gusty hour, walk the lines and re-slide every prusik. Wind is a patient loosener.

Field Recipe · Joining Lines to Reach

Makes: one long line made from two short ones — a bucket, a haul, or a ridgeline that finally reaches.

You need: two ropes or cords, and a load that is gear, not a person.

  1. Join the two lines with a double fisherman's — or, if both are webbing, a water knot with long tails.
  2. Pull the join up to working tension and inspect it: barrels face to face, tails a thumb long.
  3. Keep the join away from edges and from any point where it will be bent sharply under load.
  4. Mark the join with tape. The next person deserves to know the line has a past.

Field Recipe · Lower a Load from a Roof with a Control Line

Makes: heavy gear coming down a wall slowly, on a rope somebody controls — for things, never for people.

ComponentCount
Rope, long and sound — twice the wall height, plus working room×1
Load — a gear crate or box, tied closed×1
Short cord, for a prusik brake loop×1
Anchor beam or post you would trust with the load twice over×1
  1. Anchor the rope up top with a tensionless hitch (Entry 18) around the beam — the wraps hold the load and the short tail stays easy to untie after.
  2. Tie the load on with a round turn and two half hitches (Entry 19) around its frame or handle, and check it hangs level before it goes over the edge.
  3. Run the lowering line around a post at the top edge or hand it to your tender with a round turn around a post for friction. The tender pays line out hand over hand — a rope never wraps around a hand, ever.
  4. Clip a prusik (Entry 12) brake loop onto the loaded line and keep a hand near it: if the tender slips, the prusik grabs and the load stops instead of falling.
  5. One voice gives the calls. Lower slowly, keep every person out from under the load, and stop the moment anything shifts, creaks, or feels wrong.

Field Recipe · Rig a Shade Canopy on Four Poles

Makes: a roof of shade where there are no trees — four poles, one tarp, and a cool spot to work, cook, or sleep under.

ComponentCount
Tarp or big sheet×1
Poles, straight and of similar length×4
Cord, for lashings1 long length
Guyline cord×4
Stakes×4
  1. Build two goal-post frames on the ground: lay a crossbar across the tops of each pair of poles and join them with square lashings (Entry 15) at both crossings.
  2. Stand the frames up a tarp's length apart. Run the ridge cord from crossbar to crossbar and tie each end with a round turn and two half hitches (Entry 19).
  3. Drape the tarp over the ridge cord. Tie the corners out to stakes with guylines, each finished with a rolling hitch (Entry 14) so you can slide it and tension each corner in turn.
  4. Work around the corners twice, taking up slack evenly — a canopy fails one loose corner at a time, in the first real gust.
  5. Tie an alpine butterfly (Entry 2) in the ridge cord inside, and you have a loop that will not slide for a lantern or a hanging water bag. Tilt the low side toward the afternoon sun.

21. Stop signs

  • A knot you cannot check is a knot you cannot use. If you can't trace it and name its parts, re-tie it slower or use a Volume I knot you know cold.
  • Shock loads. Every knot here is weaker than the rope it's tied in — assume half strength, and never let a load drop and jerk any knot tight.
  • Friction hitches that were never tested. A prusik that hasn't been grip-tested is a decoration. Test, then trust.
  • The constrictor's promise. It does not untie. Anything it is around — hose, sack, or finger — gets cut free, not untied. Keep it away from skin entirely.
  • People. Again, because it matters: nothing in this book rigs a system for holding, lifting, or catching a person. Gear only.
  • Unknown rope, advanced knots. A fancy knot in rotten rope is still rotten rope. Entry 3 of Volume I outranks every entry here.

22. The whole book on one card

  • Check every knot four ways: dress it, set it, test it, back it up.
  • Alpine butterfly: the mid-line loop. Double bowline: the end loop that stays put.
  • Follow-through and directional eights: trace them flat, load them the way they point.
  • Double fisherman's joins rope; water knot joins webbing — with long tails, re-checked.
  • Zeppelin bend joins rope and still unties after a load; rolling hitch grips a line to haul along it.
  • Anchor hitch stays; constrictor never lets go; round turn lets you release under control.
  • Prusik and klemheist: slide when loose, grip when loaded — test the grip first.
  • Lashings build: square for right-angle corners, diagonal for crossings, tripod for three poles, frap everything tight.
  • Tensionless hitch: the wraps carry the load, the knot just keeps the tail honest.
  • Gear only. Never people. The pulley book is next — this one stays on the ground.
